sentences.text: No.

The Barthel Index alone is not an adequate measure of longer-term outcome after stroke because it focuses mainly on basic activities of daily living and functional independence, while missing important domains such as quality of life, mood, cognition, social participation, and caregiver burden.
It can also show ceiling effects and limited sensitivity in milder or chronic stroke.
Therefore, a comprehensive assessment should combine the Barthel Index with stroke-specific quality-of-life and multidimensional outcome measures.
The evidence is mixed.

Dedicated discharge coordinators can improve some aspects of discharge quality, such as timely discharge planning, patient education, medication reconciliation, and follow-up coordination, and some studies show reduced readmissions and length of stay.
However, results vary by setting, patient population, and how discharge quality is measured, and not all studies demonstrate clear benefit.

Yes, observational studies generally show that low serum chloride (hypochloremia) is associated with higher cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, especially in patients with heart failure, hypertension, or chronic kidney disease.
However, it may be a marker of disease severity rather than a proven independent causal risk factor, and evidence in the general population is less consistent.
No.

Studies comparing oral endotracheal intubation in helicopter versus ground environments have generally found no significant difference in success rates or time to intubation among experienced providers.
The helicopter setting may add noise, vibration, and limited space, but these factors do not appear to impair intubation efficacy when performed by trained personnel.
Yes.

Perforated appendicitis, unlike uncomplicated appendicitis, is associated with an increased risk of subsequent tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy, likely because peritoneal contamination and pelvic adhesions can damage the fallopian tubes.
The evidence comes mainly from observational studies, so it supports an association rather than proving causation.
No.

Studies of small-area variation show that carotid endarterectomy rates differ widely across regions, and these differences are largely not explained by population need (such as stroke prevalence or demographic case mix).
Instead, supply-related factors, physician practice patterns, and referral/access differences account for much of the variation.
No.
Amoxapine is a tetracyclic antidepressant, not an atypical antipsychotic, though it has some dopamine-blocking antipsychotic properties.
It is a metabolite of the antipsychotic loxapine but is classified and used primarily as an antidepressant.
Yes, laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery is feasible, especially in experienced centers.
It is technically more demanding than primary surgery because of adhesions and altered anatomy, and it carries higher rates of conversion to open surgery and perioperative complications.
Nevertheless, in carefully selected patients, laparoscopic redo fundoplication can provide good symptom control and satisfaction.
Outcomes depend heavily on surgeon expertise and appropriate preoperative workup.
No, clinician assessment alone is not accurate enough to diagnose acute chest syndrome in febrile patients with sickle cell disease.
Studies show that clinical judgment has limited sensitivity and specificity, often missing ACS or overdiagnosing it.
Therefore, objective tests such as chest radiography and oxygen saturation monitoring remain essential when ACS is suspected.
No.
When desflurane is used to control surgical stimulation during aortic surgery, studies using transesophageal echocardiography have not shown significant alteration of left ventricular function.
It generally maintains cardiac output and fractional area change, although it can affect systemic vascular resistance and heart rate.
Thus, any effect on left ventricular function appears minimal in this setting.
No, profound hypotensive events do not appear to cause myocardial ischaemic events in most patients with coronary disease.

Ambulatory monitoring studies show that ischaemic episodes are more often preceded by increases in heart rate and blood pressure rather than hypotension, though severe sustained hypotension can theoretically reduce coronary perfusion.
Yes, the NIHSS tends to favor left hemisphere strokes.
It includes items such as language and dysarthria that are more commonly impaired by left hemisphere lesions, while right hemisphere deficits like neglect are underrepresented.
Consequently, left hemisphere strokes often receive higher NIHSS scores than right hemisphere strokes of similar size or clinical severity.
No.
Routine thromboprophylaxis for every hospitalized medical patient is not justified because VTE risk varies widely and bleeding risk can offset the benefit.

Guidelines recommend risk stratification (e.g., Padua or IMPROVE VTE score plus bleeding assessment) and giving pharmacologic prophylaxis mainly to high-VTE-risk, low-bleeding-risk patients, with mechanical prophylaxis when pharmacologic prophylaxis is contraindicated.
Low-risk patients generally should not receive prophylaxis.
Yes.

The Mammography Quality Standards Act (MQSA) improved mammography quality in North Carolina by requiring accreditation, federal inspection, and minimum standards for equipment, personnel, and image quality.
Studies from the state showed better compliance and image quality after MQSA implementation, although some facilities closed and access in rural areas may have declined.
Overall, the act had a positive effect on quality while raising concerns about access.
No—abdominal CT is not always necessary in intoxicated patients with blunt trauma.

It should be used selectively based on hemodynamic stability, mechanism of injury, abdominal findings, FAST results, laboratory trends, and serial examinations, since intoxication alone is not an absolute indication.
However, because alcohol and drugs can mask intra-abdominal injury, many trauma protocols still maintain a low threshold for CT in unstable or unreliable patients.

Yes, antiphospholipid antibodies appear to contribute to an increased risk of avascular necrosis in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, although they are not the only or strongest risk factor.

Studies commonly link lupus anticoagulant and/or anticardiolipin antibodies to avascular necrosis, possibly through thrombotic microvascular occlusion, independent of or additive to corticosteroid exposure.
However, evidence is somewhat inconsistent because corticosteroids, disease activity, and other thrombophilic factors often coexist.
Thus, antiphospholipid antibodies should be considered a relevant risk factor, but their exact independent role and routine screening implications remain incompletely defined.
No, amblyopic visual loss is not always permanent.
It is often reversible with timely treatment such as patching, atropine, or corrective lenses during childhood, and some adults may improve with perceptual training.
However, if left untreated or treated after the critical period, the visual deficit can become permanent.
Yes.

Studies using anterior segment OCT show that changing from sitting to supine head/body position significantly shallows the anterior chamber in pseudoexfoliation syndrome, likely due to zonular laxity and forward movement of the lens-iris diaphragm; the effect appears greater than in normal eyes.

Yes, patients with Werlhof's disease (immune thrombocytopenic purpura) are generally considered at increased risk for bleeding complications during and after cardiac surgery, especially with cardiopulmonary bypass, because of low platelet counts, impaired platelet function, and heparin exposure.

However, the evidence is largely from case series and retrospective studies, and with aggressive perioperative management (platelet transfusions, IVIG, steroids, antifibrinolytics, and off-pump techniques when feasible), many patients can undergo surgery safely.
Thus, the risk is increased but not absolute, and outcomes depend on disease activity and perioperative strategy.

Yes—many adults with repaired tetralogy of Fallot are referred for pulmonary valve replacement too late, after years of pulmonary regurgitation have already caused advanced right ventricular dilation, dysfunction, symptoms, or arrhythmia.
Observational data show that postoperative recovery is often incomplete once severe right ventricular remodeling has occurred, suggesting earlier operation may improve outcomes.
Randomized evidence on optimal timing remains limited, but current practice frequently operates after irreversible or advanced disease has developed.

Yes, open access endoscopy can compromise informed consent; studies have found that patients referred directly for endoscopy are often less informed about the indication, alternatives, and risks than those seen in consultation first.
However, this gap is not inevitable and can be reduced with structured pre-procedure education and formal consent.
Overall, open access endoscopy risks closing the door to an adequately informed patient unless additional safeguards are used.
Yes.

Patients with rheumatoid arthritis who remain on methotrexate should generally continue folic acid supplementation long term to reduce the risk of methotrexate-related adverse effects such as oral ulcers, gastrointestinal intolerance, transaminitis, and cytopenias.
The 5 mg daily dose is higher than typically needed; many patients can be maintained on 1 mg daily, with the dose adjusted based on tolerance and laboratory results.
Folic acid can be stopped if methotrexate is discontinued.
The evidence is mixed or insufficient to call alexithymia a clear causal risk factor for unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients.
Alexithymia is consistently associated with somatization and medically unexplained symptoms in cross-sectional studies, including in general practice settings.
However, longitudinal and controlled evidence is limited, so it may be better viewed as a vulnerability marker or correlate rather than an established independent risk factor.
The evidence is mixed.

Antral follicle count generally predicts ovarian response and oocyte yield better than age and basal FSH, but for predicting live birth or ongoing pregnancy after IVF, age remains the strongest predictor and AFC adds limited independent value.
Yes, the APACHE II score is generally a reliable marker of physiological impairment in emergency surgical patients.
It quantifies acute physiological derangement through the Acute Physiology Score and has been validated for risk stratification and mortality prediction in this population.
However, its reliability can be affected by timing of assessment and ongoing treatment, so it should be used alongside clinical judgment.
No.
Longitudinal studies show that the manic/mixed distinction is not stable within individual bipolar patients; many patients switch between pure manic and mixed episodes across recurrences.
Mixed states are better considered a cross-sectional specifier rather than a persistent subtype.
Thus, an index manic or mixed episode does not reliably predict the same subtype in future episodes.
Yes, patient position can influence the risk of venous air embolism during liver surgery.

Positioning changes the height of the surgical field relative to the heart, altering the venous pressure gradient and the likelihood of air entrainment; head-up or reverse Trendelenburg positions tend to increase risk, while Trendelenburg may reduce it.
However, clinical evidence specific to liver surgery is limited and mixed, so the effect is plausible but not definitively quantified.
The evidence is mixed.

Some studies show that Medicaid managed care enrollees are more likely to report a usual source of care than uninsured low-income persons, but managed care has not consistently increased usual source of care compared with fee-for-service Medicaid.
Overall, having insurance and continuity with a provider appear to matter more than managed care itself for identifying a usual source of care.
Yes.

Aggressive use of equine-derived polyvalent antivenin for rattlesnake bites can cause serious acute hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, anaphylactoid reactions, urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension.
These immediate reactions are a major reason for pretreatment and for using more cautious, titrated dosing with modern antivenoms.
Delayed serum sickness can also occur, but the acute risks are well documented.
Yes—outcome can be predicted to some extent, but no single variable is fully reliable.

In children with malignancy and ARDS, worse outcomes are consistently associated with multiorgan dysfunction, sepsis or fungal infection, neutropenia, need for vasopressors/inotropes, higher oxygenation index or FiO2 requirements, and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
Severity scores such as PRISM/PIM and PALICC-based oxygenation metrics help stratify risk, but they are prognostic aids rather than deterministic.
Mortality remains high, and decisions should integrate dynamic clinical trajectory and underlying malignancy status.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether it is Crohn's disease.
Diagnosing Crohn's requires a combination of clinical symptoms, endoscopic findings, imaging, and histology, such as patchy transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and non-caseating granulomas.
Many other conditions, including ulcerative colitis, infectious colitis, and Behçet's disease, can mimic it.
Therefore, the diagnosis cannot be made from the question alone.
No.
In infants with a first episode of wheezing, clinical variables such as fever, tachypnea, crackles, and oxygen saturation do not reliably predict pathologic chest radiograph findings.
Because radiographic abnormalities are often nonspecific and rarely change management, routine chest radiography is generally not recommended for uncomplicated first wheezing episodes.
No.
A prospective randomized trial found that increasing the length of the trigeminal nerve within the treatment volume did not improve pain relief after radiosurgery for trigeminal neuralgia.
Instead, it was associated with a higher rate of facial numbness.
Therefore, increased nerve length does not improve outcomes and may increase complications.
No, rugby headgear does not prevent concussion.
Studies and reviews have found no reduction in concussion risk among players wearing scrum caps or padded headgear.
The gear may help reduce superficial scalp cuts and abrasions, but it does not meaningfully protect against the rotational and linear forces that cause concussive brain injury.
No.

Although hepatitis G virus (GBV-C/HGV) and TT virus (TTV) are sometimes detected in patients with cryptogenic chronic liver disease, they are also common in healthy individuals and have not been shown to cause hepatitis or chronic liver injury.
Most evidence indicates they are not meaningful causes of cryptogenic chronic liver disease, and routine testing is not recommended.
Yes.
Receipt of hospice care in nursing homes is generally associated with improved pain management at the end of life, including more frequent pain assessment and greater use of appropriate analgesics.
However, the evidence is not uniform, and pain often remains undertreated even among hospice recipients.
No.
In posterior choroidal melanoma treated with 106Ru plaques, escalating the apical dose (e.g., from 100 Gy to 150 Gy) has not been shown to improve local tumor control or eye preservation.
Higher apical doses are instead associated with more radiation retinopathy and worse visual acuity.
Therefore, routine apical dose escalation is not beneficial.
Yes.

Retinal haemorrhage is not a typical finding after convulsions alone, so its presence should prompt further evaluation for abusive head trauma, raised intracranial pressure, bleeding disorders, or other serious underlying causes.
Convulsions may coexist with or be caused by these conditions, so the combination warrants a thorough diagnostic workup rather than being attributed to seizures alone.

No, delay in transfer to a rehabilitation unit does not appear to affect mortality or functional outcome in older people after proximal femoral fracture, although it does increase the length of hospital stay.
The evidence suggests that administrative delays prolong hospitalization without changing clinical endpoints.
No.
Although a large interarm blood pressure difference (often >15–20 mm Hg) supports the diagnosis of subclavian steal, it does not reliably predict the severity of steal.
The degree of retrograde vertebral artery flow and hemodynamic significance are better assessed by duplex ultrasound, CTA/MRA, or angiography.
Clinical symptoms also do not correlate tightly with the pressure gradient alone.

Yes—admission to a tertiary center is generally associated with improved survival in elderly patients with cardiogenic shock complicating acute myocardial infarction, mainly because it enables early coronary revascularization and advanced hemodynamic support.
However, the benefit is not uniform and depends on timely presentation, comorbidity burden, and whether invasive treatment is actually delivered.
No, they do not confer exactly equal risk.
Lipids and blood pressure appear to have similar associations with myocardial infarction in women and men, but diabetes and smoking generally carry a higher relative risk in women.
Nevertheless, all four are major modifiable risk factors in both sexes, and most myocardial infarction risk is explained by these and related factors in both women and men.
No, routine antibiotics do not reliably decrease overall post-tonsillectomy morbidity.
Randomized trials and Cochrane reviews show no consistent reduction in pain or bleeding, although antibiotics may modestly reduce fever and speed return to normal activity.
Because benefits are limited and antibiotic resistance and adverse effects are concerns, routine postoperative antibiotics are not recommended.
Yes, muscle power is generally related to running speed with changes of direction, though the relationship is moderate and task-specific.
Athletes with greater lower-body power, such as higher jump performance, tend to perform better in change-of-direction tests that require rapid acceleration, braking, and re-acceleration.
However, change-of-direction speed is multifactorial and also depends on technique, reactive agility, strength, and body composition, so power alone does not fully determine performance.
No, routine pelvic CT is not necessary in most cases of renal cell carcinoma.
Standard staging typically uses CT of the chest and abdomen, with pelvic imaging reserved for symptoms, suspected pelvic metastases, or advanced disease such as inferior vena cava involvement.
Routine pelvic CT has low diagnostic yield and rarely changes management in localized RCC.
Yes, a special interest in laparoscopy affects the treatment of acute cholecystitis.
Patients treated by surgeons with this interest are more likely to undergo laparoscopic cholecystectomy, have a lower conversion rate to open surgery, and shorter hospital stays.
However, overall complication and mortality rates appear similar to those treated by surgeons without this special interest.
Yes, hippocampal mossy fibers can release GABA, though they are primarily glutamatergic.
A subset of dentate gyrus granule cells expresses GABAergic markers, and their axons can co-release GABA onto CA3 pyramidal cells and interneurons.
This GABAergic transmission is typically weaker than the glutamatergic component and may be more prominent in developing or epileptic tissue.
Yes, increased neutrophil migratory activity after major trauma is thought to be a contributing factor in the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
Trauma primes neutrophils and can enhance their chemotaxis and migration, promoting pulmonary neutrophil sequestration and alveolar-capillary injury.
However, ARDS is multifactorial, so this increased migratory activity acts as one important mechanism rather than the sole cause.
Yes.

In newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, lower fasting plasma glucose at diagnosis is generally associated with milder disease and lower risks of microvascular and cardiovascular complications and mortality compared with higher levels.
This association is observational and may be partly explained by earlier detection and less severe disease, so causality is uncertain.
The evidence is insufficient to say that withdrawal-induced anxiety in alcoholism is based on beta-endorphin deficiency.
Beta-endorphin and endogenous opioid changes may contribute, but withdrawal anxiety is primarily linked to GABA/glutamate dysregulation, CRF activation, and other stress-system adaptations.
Yes, HELLP syndrome is generally considered a severe variant of pre-eclampsia that provides evidence for an exaggerated systemic inflammatory response.
It is associated with elevated inflammatory cytokines, complement activation, and endothelial dysfunction.
However, the precise contribution of inflammation versus placental ischemia and angiogenic imbalance remains debated.
Overall, HELLP supports the concept that systemic inflammation is part of the pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia, but it is not solely an inflammatory disorder.
Yes, ultrasound imaging before puncture facilitates internal jugular vein cannulation.
Pre-puncture scanning helps identify the vein's location, depth, and anatomic variations, which can improve first-attempt success and reduce complications compared with landmark techniques.
However, real-time ultrasound guidance during needle insertion is generally superior to pre-puncture imaging alone and is the preferred approach.
No—routine childhood circumcision is not recommended, though it may be elected for specific medical, cultural, or religious reasons.
Major pediatric bodies find that health benefits (e.g., reduced UTI, HIV, and penile cancer risks) outweigh risks but do not justify universal circumcision.
The decision should be individualized and made by parents/caregivers with medical guidance, considering the child's best interests.
In high-HIV settings, voluntary medical male circumcision is recommended for adolescents and adults, not as a routine childhood procedure.
No.
Studies specifically in hip arthroplasty have not found that ibuprofen significantly increases perioperative blood loss or transfusion requirements.
Ibuprofen can reversibly impair platelet function, but this has not translated into a consistent clinically important bleeding risk in this setting.
Evidence is limited, so caution is still warranted with concurrent anticoagulants.
No, a written information sheet did not improve recall by patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty.
In a randomized study, patients who received the written information sheet had recall similar to those who did not.
Recall of risks and benefits was generally poor in both groups, suggesting that written information alone is insufficient for informed consent.
The evidence is mixed/limited: anorectal endosonography is not routinely valuable in dyschezia, but it can be helpful in selected patients with suspected sphincter defects or prior anal surgery.
Functional causes of dyschezia are better assessed with anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion testing, and defecography.
It should not be used as a first-line test for dyschezia.
The evidence is mixed.
Higher BMI is generally associated with increased intraoperative difficulty and postoperative morbidity, such as anastomotic leakage and wound complications, after gastrectomy.

However, for long-term survival, low BMI or underweight is more consistently linked to worse prognosis, while overweight or mild obesity sometimes shows a protective association (the obesity paradox).
These relationships are confounded by stage, nutritional status, and treatment factors, so BMI alone does not clearly determine long-term outcomes.
Yes—environmental factors are important in primary systemic vasculitis, although their role varies by subtype and they usually act together with genetic susceptibility.

Recognized contributors include infections such as Staphylococcus aureus in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, silica dust and other occupational exposures, certain drugs like hydralazine and propylthiouracil, smoking, and possibly pollutants or seasonal and geographic patterns.

They can trigger or modulate disease onset and relapse, but no single environmental cause explains most cases, so the evidence points most strongly to gene–environment interaction rather than a purely environmental etiology.
Yes, observational studies generally show that specialty cardiology care is associated with improved survival in patients with congestive heart failure.
This benefit appears partly mediated by greater use of guideline-directed medical therapy such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers, and it is stronger in patients with reduced ejection fraction.
However, because most evidence is non-randomized, confounding by disease severity and referral bias means the causal effect of specialty care itself remains uncertain.
Yes, tumor depth should generally be included in prognostication for soft tissue sarcoma.
Depth relative to the superficial fascia is a standard component of AJCC/UICC staging for extremity and trunk sarcomas, with deep tumors associated with worse outcomes.
It also adds prognostic information in several validated nomograms, though its independent value may vary by histologic subtype and anatomic site.
Therefore, it is reasonable to include depth alongside size, grade, and other factors.
Yes, but it is a rare sequela.

Case reports have described spinal subdural hematoma after rupture of an intracranial aneurysm, likely from blood extending from the intracranial subarachnoid space into the spinal subdural compartment or from related pressure changes.
It should be considered in a patient with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage who develops back pain or progressive myelopathy.
The evidence is mixed.
Neuronal loss in mesial temporal sclerosis has been linked to apoptotic markers such as TUNEL positivity and caspase activation, but excitotoxic necrosis also contributes.
In chronic human surgical specimens, pure apoptosis is uncommon, and the sclerosis likely reflects a combination of apoptotic and necrotic cell death.
Thus, apoptosis is involved but is not the sole mechanism.
Yes, but only in selected patients after individualized risk-benefit assessment.

Anticoagulation may be resumed after intracerebral hemorrhage when the thromboembolic risk from the underlying condition (e.g., mechanical heart valve, atrial fibrillation) outweighs the risk of recurrent bleeding.
Timing varies from a few days for high-risk mechanical valves to weeks or longer for atrial fibrillation, and alternatives such as left atrial appendage closure may be considered.
Guidelines recommend multidisciplinary decision-making rather than routine immediate or permanent avoidance.
Yes—socioeconomic status generally matters for quality of life in lung cancer patients, though the evidence is somewhat mixed.
Lower socioeconomic status is consistently linked to worse health-related quality of life, greater symptom burden, and more psychological distress.
These associations are partly explained by later stage at diagnosis, reduced access to timely treatment, financial toxicity, and more comorbidities.
However, the strength of the relationship varies by how socioeconomic status and quality of life are measured and by adjustment for clinical factors.

Yes, first-line single-agent mitoxantrone appears to be as effective as combination chemotherapy in high-risk metastatic breast cancer patients in terms of overall response and survival, based on randomized trial evidence.
The main advantage is reduced toxicity, including less alopecia, nausea, and vomiting.
However, combination regimens may still produce somewhat higher response rates and longer time to progression, so the choice should be individualized.
No, progression of valvar aortic stenosis cannot currently be predicted accurately for an individual patient.
The rate of progression is highly variable and is influenced by clinical, hemodynamic, and biomarker factors, but these explain only a limited portion of the variability.
Available models and risk markers have modest predictive value and are not reliable enough to guide individual timing of intervention.
Therefore, regular clinical and echocardiographic surveillance remains necessary rather than relying on predicted progression.
Yes—in rodent studies, Nd:YAG laser-induced thermotherapy can produce locoregional, reversible opening of the blood-brain barrier and increase paclitaxel delivery to brain tissue.
This supports the concept as a potential adjuvant approach for glioma, because paclitaxel normally has poor blood-brain barrier penetration.
However, the evidence remains preclinical, and safety, reproducibility, and clinical benefit in humans are unproven.
Yes.
Communication with terminally ill patients can be taught and improved through structured training such as workshops, role-play, and feedback.
Such programs typically increase clinicians' confidence, knowledge, and observable communication skills.
Evidence for direct improvements in patient-reported outcomes is more mixed, and skills may need reinforcement over time.
Yes, a 9-month regimen is generally sufficient for tuberculous enterocolitis.
Standard anti-tuberculosis therapy for drug-susceptible intestinal TB is typically 6 months, so 9 months is adequate and often used for extensive or slow-responding disease.
Treatment should be individualized, but 9 months is not considered insufficient in most guidelines.
No.
In studies of early postpartum discharge with nurse home visits, the adequacy of newborn metabolic screening has generally been similar to that with standard discharge.
The home visits help ensure that any needed repeat or timely screening is completed, so early discharge with this support does not appear to compromise screening adequacy.
Without nurse home visits, early discharge might increase the risk of inadequate screening.
No.

Studies comparing clinical examination with objective measures show that practicing surgeons often cannot reliably detect early or subclinical lymphedema because swelling may be minimal and easily missed.
Reliable detection generally requires validated tools such as bioimpedance spectroscopy or perometry, often with referral to a lymphedema specialist.
No, routine double reading of barium enemas is not necessary.
While a second reader may occasionally detect additional polyps, it rarely alters management for clinically significant lesions like cancer, and the added cost and time are not justified.
Therefore, single reading by an experienced radiologist remains the standard practice.
Yes, breast cancer survival has improved significantly in many high-income countries over recent decades, largely due to earlier detection and better treatments.
For example, 5-year relative survival for localized breast cancer is now about 99% in the United States, and overall breast cancer mortality has declined.
However, gains are not uniform: survival remains lower for metastatic disease, aggressive subtypes like triple-negative breast cancer, and underserved populations.
Thus, the overall evidence indicates improving survival, but with important disparities and global variation.

Yes—there is a favorable subset of patients with oligometastatic prostate cancer, typically those with hormone-sensitive disease, limited (often ≤5) metastases, metachronous recurrence, lymph-node-only or bone-only involvement, low PSA, and no visceral metastases.
These patients can have prolonged survival and may benefit from metastasis-directed therapy or deferred systemic therapy.
However, favorable outcomes are not universal, so risk stratification by tumor volume, timing, and biology is essential.
Yes.

Pain is a clinically relevant problem in general adult psychiatry because it is highly prevalent in patients with depression, anxiety, trauma-related, and somatic symptom disorders, and it often worsens psychiatric symptoms, functioning, and quality of life.
Pain can also complicate diagnosis and treatment, increase disability and healthcare utilization, and may arise from or interact with psychotropic medications.
Therefore, routine assessment and integrated management of pain are important in psychiatric practice.
No, the available evidence suggests that sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma is not clinically meaningful.

Most studies show that the extent of surgical resection is the dominant prognostic factor, while the histological distinction between pilocytic and diffuse astrocytoma does not significantly affect progression-free or overall survival.

Although some series report slightly worse outcomes for diffuse subtypes, this difference is typically not statistically significant and does not alter management when gross total resection is achieved.

Yes, CT can often predict the level of CSF block in tuberculous hydrocephalus, mainly by assessing fourth ventricular size and basal cistern enhancement; a normal fourth ventricle suggests aqueductal obstruction, while a dilated fourth ventricle suggests a more distal (outlet or communicating) block.
However, CT is not perfectly accurate, and MRI or contrast cisternography may be needed when the level is ambiguous.
Yes.

The sequence of clamp application can influence distal embolisation during open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair; clamping the proximal aorta before the distal iliac arteries is generally recommended to reduce the risk of dislodging mural thrombus or atheroma into the legs.
However, high-level randomized evidence is limited, and some studies have not shown a clear difference.

Yes, fear of anaphylactic shock has been a recognized barrier to wider adoption of percutaneous and laparoscopic techniques for liver hydatid cysts, but the evidence suggests this fear is often disproportionate.
The actual incidence of anaphylaxis is low (around 1% or less) and can be minimized with scolicidal agents, albendazole prophylaxis, and careful patient selection.
Therefore, while fear may discourage some surgeons, it should not be a major obstacle to adopting these minimally invasive approaches.
No—differential symptom reporting does not fully account for the higher rates of depression in women.

Although men may underreport and women may be more willing to disclose symptoms, the female preponderance persists in studies using structured diagnostic interviews, clinician ratings, and symptom inventories.
Biological, hormonal, and psychosocial factors likely contribute.
Reporting bias may modestly affect estimates but is not the main explanation.
The evidence is mixed.
Dietitians and nurses often agree on general diabetes nutrition principles, such as reducing refined sugars and eating regular meals.

However, they may differ in specific recommendations—dietitians typically provide more detailed, individualized medical nutrition therapy, while nurses may focus on practical or general dietary guidance.
As a result, patients can receive inconsistent messages depending on whom they ask.
No.
Studies of women treated with radiotherapy for Hodgkin's disease have not found that radiation around the time of pregnancy significantly modifies the subsequent risk of breast cancer.
The increased breast cancer risk in these patients is primarily driven by younger age at treatment and higher radiation dose to the breast.
Yes.
The Omega-3 Index (red blood cell EPA+DHA) is associated with lower risk of death from coronary heart disease, especially sudden cardiac death, and has been proposed as a new risk factor.
However, randomized trials of omega-3 supplementation have shown mixed effects on CHD mortality, so it is best viewed as a strong risk marker rather than a proven causal factor.
No, acute changes in heart rate induced by isoproterenol do not appear to affect aortic stiffness in patients with hypertension.

Studies using isoproterenol infusion to raise heart rate while measuring carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity found no significant change in aortic PWV, despite increases in heart rate and decreases in mean arterial pressure.
This suggests that aortic stiffness in hypertension is not acutely heart-rate dependent under these conditions.
No, peer review is not a reliable or valid method for profiling quality of care.
Studies show poor inter-rater reliability and weak correlation with explicit quality criteria, and it identifies more patients as having poor quality than explicit measures do.
It should not be used as a primary method for profiling, though it may have other roles in quality improvement.
Yes.
Sports medicine journals publish peer-reviewed research on injury prevention, rehabilitation, exercise physiology, and performance that directly informs practitioners and athletes.
However, applicability can vary by sport, level, and setting, and access or implementation barriers may limit direct use.
Overall, they are relevant and applicable, especially when used to support evidence-based practice and training decisions.
Yes, preclinical studies indicate that c-Kit can support uveal melanoma cell growth and that inhibiting it reduces proliferation, so it is a potential therapeutic target.

However, activating KIT mutations are uncommon and clinical trials of KIT inhibitors in metastatic uveal melanoma have shown limited benefit, so its role as a broadly effective target remains unproven.
Yes.
In 4-year follow-up studies, the type of remission after a major depressive episode is an important risk factor for relapse.
Patients with partial remission or residual symptoms have significantly higher relapse/recurrence rates than those in full remission.
Full remission or recovery is associated with a lower risk, making remission status a key prognostic factor.
The evidence is mixed: reducing spasticity can produce functional benefit in some patients, but it does not reliably translate into improved active function.
Spasticity reduction often helps passive functions such as positioning, hygiene, comfort, and ease of care, and may improve range of motion or gait in selected cases.
However, active gains in walking, arm use, or transfers are variable and depend on the underlying diagnosis, treatment goal, and whether the patient relies on spasticity for support.
Therefore, functional benefit should be assessed individually rather than assumed from a reduction in spasticity alone.
Yes, the concept of an early adopter of drugs exists in substance-use research, especially for novel psychoactive substances.
Studies describe a subset of users who try new drugs earlier than the general population, often experienced polydrug users with high novelty-seeking and strong drug-network connections.
However, it is a descriptive, not diagnostic, category, and its boundaries and predictive value remain debated.
Yes.

DCIS diagnosis, grading, margin assessment, and distinction from atypical ductal hyperplasia or microinvasion show substantial interobserver variability, and expert breast pathology review can change both the diagnosis and the treatment plan.
Therefore, expert breast pathology assessment is generally considered necessary for optimal, guideline-concordant management of DCIS.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that adding 2-methoxyestradiol reliably reduces chemotherapy doses in human ovarian cancer.
Preclinical studies suggest it can enhance the activity of agents such as paclitaxel or cisplatin, raising the possibility of a dose-sparing effect.
However, clinical data are limited and not definitive, so chemotherapy dose reduction should not be assumed outside a clinical trial.
The evidence is mixed.

Increased private health care use can substitute for some NHS-funded elective care and may shorten NHS waiting lists for those procedures, especially for patients paying out-of-pocket or using insurance.

However, it often represents additional consumption rather than a direct substitute, and it may not reduce overall NHS demand because patients still rely on the NHS for emergency, complex, and follow-up care.
No.
Studies of radical perineal prostatectomy have found that a prior benign prostate biopsy does not independently predict adverse pathologic findings or biochemical recurrence.
Patients with and without prior negative biopsies have similar outcomes after surgery, so prior benign biopsy status should not be used to estimate prognosis in this setting.

Yes, socioeconomic status matters for postpartum learning needs, though the effect is mainly on which topics are prioritized and how information is accessed rather than on whether women have any learning needs.

Women with lower socioeconomic status often report greater needs around infant care, breastfeeding, contraception, and community resources, and they face more barriers such as low health literacy and limited access.
Higher socioeconomic status women may focus more on self-care, mental health, and return-to-work issues.
Overall, postpartum education should be tailored to socioeconomic context while recognizing that many core learning needs are universal.
The evidence is mixed.
Adjuvant radiation for stage III thymoma is not universally necessary after complete resection, but it is often considered for incomplete resection or positive margins to improve local control.
It has not consistently shown an overall survival benefit, so treatment should be individualized.
No clear difference has been demonstrated.

Inhaled corticosteroids are more effective than cromones for improving lung function and symptoms in children with chronic asthma, but randomized trials and reviews have not found a statistically significant difference in hospital admission rates.
Hospital admissions are relatively rare in these trials, so the evidence may be underpowered for that outcome.
Yes—serum pancreatic lipase is generally preferred over amylase for diagnosing acute pancreatitis because it is more sensitive and specific and stays elevated longer.
Major guidelines recommend lipase when available, and it can replace amylase without loss of diagnostic accuracy.
Amylase remains an acceptable alternative if lipase is unavailable or delayed.
Neither marker alone establishes severity or etiology, so clinical context and imaging still matter.
Yes.
Injury mortality rates vary widely across U.S. states, with some states consistently higher or lower than others.
For example, unintentional injury and drug overdose deaths tend to be higher in many rural, Appalachian, and Western states and lower in some Northeastern and urban states.
These differences reflect demographics, occupation, access to care, firearm prevalence, opioid prescribing, and state policies.
The evidence is mixed but suggests that frequent fast-food consumption may be associated with a higher risk or severity of asthma, especially in children and adolescents.

Observational studies, mostly cross-sectional, show associations with asthma symptoms, but causality is not established and results are confounded by obesity, socioeconomic status, and other lifestyle factors.
Fast food may plausibly contribute through obesity, systemic inflammation, high saturated fat and salt intake, and low antioxidant intake, but more longitudinal research is needed.
Yes, there is evidence for a potential role.
Uterine natural killer cells are regulated by sex hormones, and menopausal hormone therapy can increase their presence in the endometrium.

These cells produce angiogenic factors and cytokines that may influence vascular stability, and some studies link altered uNK cell populations to irregular bleeding on HRT, although the evidence is not definitive.
No.
Bedside swallowing assessments after acute stroke are useful for triage but have limited sensitivity and cannot reliably exclude aspiration.
Silent aspiration is common, and patients who pass a bedside screen may still aspirate on instrumental testing.
Therefore, videofluoroscopic swallow study or FEES is recommended when aspiration risk is a concern.

Yes—homebrew BCR-ABL1 qRT-PCR assays can produce results that correlate with standard or commercial assays, but only when they are rigorously validated and calibrated against the WHO International Standard to report on the International Scale.
Without such standardization, homebrew assays often show good correlation within a laboratory but poor interlaboratory comparability and may not be interchangeable for clinical monitoring.
So correlation is possible, but not guaranteed or clinically transferable by default.
The evidence is mixed.

Many studies show grandmultiparous women (parity ≥5) have higher rates of preterm birth, low birth weight, perinatal mortality, and maternal complications, and some adjusted analyses find these associations persist.

However, other studies find the association is largely explained by confounders such as advanced maternal age, socioeconomic status, BMI, and interpregnancy interval, so grandmultiparity is not consistently an independent risk factor.
Yes, in strabismic amblyopia, Landolt C acuity is often better than Snellen E acuity.
This difference is thought to reflect stronger crowding and contour interaction effects for the Snellen E optotype in strabismic amblyopia.
In contrast, anisometropic amblyopia typically shows more similar acuity with both tests.
Yes.

A study found that the arginine vasopressin V1a receptor (AVPR1A) microsatellite RS1 was significantly associated with hypersexuality in children with a prepubertal and early adolescent bipolar disorder phenotype.
This suggested that AVPR1A variation may contribute to hypersexuality in this population, though the finding was preliminary and requires replication.
Yes, end-tidal CO2 generally correlates with arterial CO2 in extremely low birth weight infants during the first week of life, but the correlation is only moderate.
The relationship is limited by variable dead-space ventilation, pulmonary disease, and shunting.
Therefore, EtCO2 is more useful for trend monitoring than as a substitute for arterial blood gas measurements, and absolute values should be confirmed with blood gases.
No.
In academic vascular departments, residents' continuity of care is often fragmented, with trainees frequently missing parts of the preoperative, postoperative, and follow-up phases.
Consequently, many do not consistently learn the full spectrum of longitudinal surgical care for vascular patients.
The evidence is mixed.

Cytokine concentrations in pancreatic juice, such as IL-8, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and MCP-1, are often elevated in chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer compared with controls, and some studies report associations with disease presence.
However, findings are inconsistent across studies, with overlapping values and lack of validation, so pancreatic-juice cytokines are not established as reliable predictors of pancreatic disease.
They remain research biomarkers rather than clinically useful diagnostic tests.
Yes, greater obstructive sleep apnea severity, especially higher apnea-hypopnea index, is generally associated with needing a higher continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) level.
However, the relationship is only moderate, so baseline severity alone cannot reliably predict the exact pressure a patient will require.
Other factors such as body mass index, neck circumference, and upper airway anatomy also influence CPAP requirements.
Therefore, severity is a useful predictor but not a substitute for CPAP titration.

Yes—preoperative tracheobronchoscopy can matter in newborns with esophageal atresia because it helps localize the tracheoesophageal fistula, detect additional or proximal fistulas, and identify associated airway anomalies such as tracheomalacia or laryngeal clefts.
These findings can alter surgical planning and anesthetic management, especially for thoracoscopic repair or when the fistula is uncertain.
However, its routine use remains debated, and it is most clearly valuable when imaging is equivocal or complex airway/fistula anatomy is suspected.
The evidence is mixed.

Several randomized trials and meta-analyses suggest that hydrophilic guidewires can improve technical success in peripheral PTA, especially for crossing complex or occlusive lesions, but a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to confirm a statistically significant overall improvement.

Therefore, while hydrophilic guidewires are widely used and may be beneficial, the current evidence does not conclusively show a significant improvement in technical success rates for all peripheral PTA.
No—available evidence indicates that histological features such as hemorrhage, necrosis, or fibrosis do not consistently correlate with the clinical presentation or outcome of pituitary apoplexy.
Clinical severity and prognosis appear to be driven more by the extent of the apoplectic event and the timing of treatment than by specific histopathological findings.
Therefore, histology alone should not be used to predict presentation or outcome.
No.
Routine chest radiography after transbronchial biopsy is generally not necessary in asymptomatic patients, because clinically significant pneumothorax is uncommon and usually produces symptoms.
Imaging should be reserved for patients who develop symptoms, have risk factors, or have an otherwise complicated procedure.

Yes—French lay people and health professionals generally find it acceptable to breach confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease, especially when the risk of transmission is high and the patient refuses to inform her.
However, acceptability is not absolute; it varies with factors such as the severity of the disease and the likelihood of transmission.
Yes, there is a difference.

A comparison of 500 prefilled textured saline implants and 500 standard textured saline implants found that prefilled implants had a significantly higher deflation rate (roughly 7–8%) than standard implants (roughly 3%).
This difference contributed to the discontinuation of prefilled saline breast implants.
No, decisional algorithms cannot fully replace global introspection in individual causality assessment of spontaneously reported ADRs.
They improve standardization, reproducibility, and transparency, but they often oversimplify complex clinical data and show only moderate agreement with expert judgment.
Global introspection remains essential for integrating temporal, biological, and clinical context, so algorithms should be used as aids rather than replacements.
No, the skepticism is not broadly justified.

In advanced non-small cell lung cancer, platinum-based chemotherapy improves overall survival compared with best supportive care, with a modest median gain of about 1–2 months and roughly a 10% absolute improvement in 1-year survival, while also providing palliative benefit.
However, because the benefit is small and varies by performance status and molecular subtype, skepticism remains reasonable for frail patients or when targeted or immunotherapy options are available.
Yes, fetal gender is associated with emergency department visits for asthma during pregnancy.
Women carrying a female fetus appear to have a higher risk of asthma exacerbations, including ED visits, compared with those carrying a male fetus.
However, some studies have not found a consistent association, so the evidence is not entirely uniform.
The evidence is mixed.
Most studies show that many uterine myomas do not significantly grow during pregnancy, and some even shrink, although a subset—often larger ones—may enlarge, especially in the first trimester.
Therefore, the traditional belief that myomas universally grow during pregnancy is not supported.
Yes.

Multiple studies in non-small-cell lung cancer show that baseline self-reported health-related quality of life, especially global quality of life, physical functioning, fatigue, and appetite loss, independently predicts overall survival after adjusting for clinical and tumor factors.
Therefore, health-related quality of life should be considered a prognostic marker in this population.
Yes.

Patients with diabetes mellitus tend to have more complex coronary lesions, including multivessel disease, longer and more diffuse stenoses, heavier calcification, bifurcation involvement, and chronic total occlusions.
This greater anatomic complexity contributes to higher procedural difficulty and worse cardiovascular outcomes after revascularization.
No—routine frozen section generally does not alter surgical management of multinodular thyroid disease.

Decisions about lobectomy versus total thyroidectomy are usually based on preoperative FNA, ultrasound findings, symptoms, and the extent of bilateral disease, while frozen section is unreliable for distinguishing follicular adenoma from carcinoma.
It may occasionally change management when it confirms unexpected malignancy or gross invasion, but its routine use in multinodular disease is not supported.
No, supervised colorectal trainees do not appear to differ significantly from consultants in the quality of TME surgery.
Studies comparing supervised trainee-performed TME with consultant-performed TME generally show comparable rates of complete mesorectal excision and similar oncological quality.
Any differences are usually limited to longer operative times rather than worse TME grading.
However, most evidence is retrospective, so minor differences cannot be entirely excluded.
Yes, obstructive sleep apnea is associated with reduced aerobic fitness, though the relationship is partly confounded by obesity and cardiometabolic disease.
Intermittent hypoxia, sleep fragmentation, and sympathetic activation can impair cardiovascular and skeletal muscle function, lowering VO2max and exercise tolerance.
Treatment with CPAP may improve some exercise-related measures, but improvements in aerobic fitness are not consistently demonstrated.
No, fluoroscopy is not essential for retrieval of lower ureteric stones.
Ureteroscopy for distal ureteral stones can be performed safely using direct vision and a guidewire, with or without fluoroscopic guidance.
Fluoroscopy is commonly used for navigation and safety, but alternatives such as ultrasound or no imaging are feasible in selected cases.
Therefore, it is helpful but not mandatory.
Yes, endoaortic balloon occlusion can be safe in selected patients with atherosclerotic ascending aorta, but it is not universally risk-free.

It avoids external cross-clamping and may reduce embolic risk when guided by epiaortic ultrasound, yet it still carries risks of stroke, aortic dissection, and rupture, particularly with severe, mobile, or circumferential plaque.
Careful patient selection and intraoperative imaging are essential, and severe atherosclerosis or porcelain aorta may be a contraindication.
The evidence is mixed.

Some observational studies and meta-analyses suggest that periconceptional folic acid supplementation may reduce the risk of congenital heart defects, particularly atrioventricular septal defects, in children with Down syndrome, but other studies have found no significant association.
Folic acid does not prevent Down syndrome itself, and randomized controlled trials are lacking.
Yes.
Stretch-sensitive KCNQ1 mutations have been proposed as a mechanistic link between genetic susceptibility and environmental factors in atrial fibrillation.

In experimental studies, such mutations can sensitize IKs to membrane stretch, so hemodynamic stress or atrial dilation promotes a gain-of-function potassium current that shortens atrial action potentials and favors reentry.
This supports a gene–environment interaction model for AF, though the evidence is strongest for specific KCNQ1 variants and does not explain all AF pathogenesis.
No.

A comparison study found that although long-term continence was similar, the transanal pull-through was associated with significantly higher rates of postoperative enterocolitis and soiling than the transabdominal pull-through.
Therefore, the long-term results are not equal.

Yes, size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement can still be considered a niche option in modern aortic surgery, particularly in selected high-risk or elderly patients when full ascending aortic replacement is judged too risky.
It is not standard first-line therapy, however, because of concerns about long-term durability, redilation, and reoperation.
Most contemporary practice favors ascending aortic replacement when intervention is indicated, especially in patients with connective tissue disease or more extensive aortic pathology.
The evidence supporting aortoplasty is limited mainly to retrospective series, so it should be individualized.
The evidence is mixed.

Neck dissection is often recommended as part of combined-modality therapy for resectable cervical nodal metastasis from an unknown head and neck primary, but definitive radiotherapy or chemoradiation is an acceptable alternative in selected patients, and its impact on overall survival remains debated.
Yes, though their clinical effects overlap.

Bile duct sludge is often a transient or precursor state that can resolve spontaneously, whereas bile duct stones are more likely to persist and cause recurrent obstruction, cholangitis, or pancreatitis requiring endoscopic or surgical extraction.
However, sludge is not benign and can cause the same complications, especially microlithiasis-related pancreatitis, so symptomatic cases may still need ERCP.
Yes, renal warm ischemia over 30 minutes during laparoscopic partial nephrectomy is possible and does occur, especially with complex or hilar tumors.
However, it is generally avoided because prolonged warm ischemia beyond 30 minutes is associated with a higher risk of acute kidney injury and long-term renal dysfunction.
Most surgeons aim to keep warm ischemia time under 20–25 minutes when feasible.
No, ambulatory process of care does not reliably predict health-related quality of life outcomes in patients with chronic disease.
Studies generally find weak or inconsistent associations between process measures and HRQoL after adjusting for patient characteristics.
Some condition-specific process measures may show modest correlations, but overall process of care explains little of the variation in HRQoL.
The evidence is mixed: breast cancer prognosis is not inherited in a simple Mendelian sense, but inherited genetic factors can influence tumor biology and survival.
Germline mutations such as BRCA1/2 affect cancer risk and may be associated with prognosis, and some common variants have been linked to survival differences.
However, prognosis is predominantly determined by tumor stage, grade, receptor status (ER/PR/HER2), and treatment.
Overall, inherited factors explain only a limited portion of variability in breast cancer outcomes.
No.
The study found that an advertisement targeting the tobacco industry did not significantly affect young people's perceptions of smoking in movies or their intention to smoke.
Any measurable effects were limited to attitudes toward the tobacco industry rather than the movie-smoking or smoking-intention outcomes.
The evidence is mixed or insufficient to say that working in a rural location by itself reduces midwives' competence.

Rural midwives often develop broad autonomy and strong generalist experience, but they may have less access to continuing education, peer review, and rare emergency case exposure, which can affect maintenance of specific skills.
Competence appears more closely tied to training opportunities, case volume, and support systems than to rurality alone.
Yes, studies among African Americans with acute myocardial infarction suggest gender differences in reasons for delay, though the evidence is limited.
African American women more often delay because they do not recognize symptoms as cardiac, attribute them to non-cardiac causes, or prioritize caregiving responsibilities.
African American men more often delay due to denial, minimizing symptoms, or believing the symptoms will resolve on their own.
Some reasons, such as mistrust of the healthcare system and not wanting to bother others, overlap between genders.
Yes, reading comprehension ability in adults with mild intellectual disabilities can be improved, though the evidence base is limited and gains are often modest and variable.
Targeted, explicit instruction in comprehension strategies such as question generation, summarization, and reciprocal teaching can produce measurable gains.
Improvements tend to be greater when instruction is individualized, uses real-life texts, and provides repeated practice with feedback.
More high-quality studies in adults are needed to determine optimal duration and long-term maintenance.
No, the evidence indicates that serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activity is not associated with the frequency of severe hypoglycaemia in Type 1 diabetes.
Studies measuring serum ACE in patients with and without recurrent severe hypoglycaemia have found no significant difference.
While ACE gene polymorphisms may influence hypoglycaemia risk, serum ACE levels themselves do not appear to be a useful marker for severe hypoglycaemia frequency.
No.

Family history of premature cardiovascular disease or familial hypercholesterolemia is useful but has low sensitivity for identifying children with elevated cholesterol, and many affected children have negative or unknown family histories.

Therefore, family history alone is not reliable for choosing which school children to screen; universal or broader screening is recommended, with selective screening only when universal screening is not feasible.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient for a spine-specific effect, but general surgical guidelines recommend against razor shaving because it can cause microabrasions and increase surgical site infection risk.
If hair removal is needed, clipping immediately before surgery or leaving hair in place is preferred.
No.
Maternal death audit is used in both high- and low-income settings, so the difference is not simply rich versus poor.

High-income countries often rely on confidential enquiries and comprehensive civil registration, while low- and middle-income countries more often use facility-based maternal death reviews or verbal autopsy, with variable completeness and impact.
The key determinants are health-system capacity, data quality, political will, and implementation, not income level alone.
No.

In patients with locally advanced urothelial carcinoma treated with adjuvant M-VEC chemotherapy, HER2 immunoreactivity has been reported not to correlate significantly with disease-free or overall survival.
It also did not remain an independent prognostic factor in multivariate analysis in that setting.
Thus, HER2 immunoreactivity does not appear to provide prognostic information for this specific patient group, though results in other urothelial carcinoma settings are mixed.
Yes, but only partially and with limited accuracy.
Preoperative factors such as younger age, female sex, anxiety, pain catastrophizing, chronic pain, opioid use, and type of surgery are consistently associated with higher postoperative pain.

Several predictive models and risk scores have been developed, but they generally explain only a modest portion of variability and are not yet reliable enough to replace individualized clinical assessment.
Yes, adjuvant aromatase inhibitors are associated with a modestly increased cardiovascular risk compared with tamoxifen in postmenopausal women with early breast cancer.
Meta-analyses show about an 18% relative increase in cardiovascular events, mainly angina and myocardial infarction, though the absolute risk is small.
This risk is less clear when aromatase inhibitors are compared with placebo, and they reduce thromboembolic events.
Cardiovascular risk should therefore be weighed against efficacy and thromboembolic risk when selecting adjuvant endocrine therapy.
No.

Histologic evaluation of the testicular remnant in vanishing testes syndrome typically shows only fibrous tissue, calcification, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages, with no viable germ cells or malignant potential.
Therefore, surgical excision of the remnant is not routinely necessary.
Yes.
In winter oil-seed rape, cold acclimation is associated with changes in cell wall pectins, including altered pectin content, degree of methylation/esterification, and pectin methylesterase activity.
De-acclimation generally reverses these pectin-related changes, consistent with pectins contributing to cell wall remodeling during freezing tolerance.
Therefore, pectins are involved in both cold acclimation and de-acclimation in this species.
No.

Specialised phonological awareness training is not indicated for every preschool child; it is generally reserved for children at risk for reading difficulties, such as those with language impairment, family history of dyslexia, or identified weaknesses on screening.

Universal preschool instruction can include phonological awareness activities, but intensive or specialised training for all children is not supported as necessary and may divert resources from those who need it most.
Yes.

Adding body diffusion-weighted imaging to nonenhanced T2-weighted MRI improves detection of endometrial cancer, as tumors typically show high signal on high-b-value DWI and low ADC, increasing contrast against surrounding tissues.

It is especially useful when contrast-enhanced MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, though normal endometrium can also be bright on DWI, particularly in premenopausal women, which may reduce specificity.
The evidence is mixed: routine laboratory markers can raise suspicion but cannot reliably distinguish nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) from alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) on their own.
An AST/ALT ratio >2, elevated GGT, macrocytosis (high MCV), and increased IgA tend to favor alcohol-related liver injury, whereas NASH often shows AST/ALT <1 and milder GGT/MCV changes.
However, these findings overlap substantially, especially in advanced fibrosis, and no routine marker or simple panel has adequate sensitivity and specificity for a definitive diagnosis.
Liver biopsy remains the reference standard, and clinical history plus the overall pattern of injury are still essential.
No, chest wall irradiation should not be routinely included after mastectomy for node-negative breast cancer.
For most T1–T2 N0 tumors with clear margins, postmastectomy radiation is omitted because the local recurrence risk is low.
It may be considered or recommended in selected high-risk node-negative cases, such as T3/T4 tumors, positive or close margins, or other adverse features.
The decision should therefore be individualized based on tumor size, margin status, and other risk factors.
No—low-tone sudden deafness does not inevitably progress to Meniere's disease.
It is often linked to endolymphatic hydrops and may be an early or atypical form in some patients, but many recover fully or partially and never develop classic Meniere's.
Long-term studies suggest only a minority—roughly 10–30%—eventually meet criteria for Meniere's disease, especially those with recurrent attacks, vertigo, or fluctuating hearing.
Prognosis is therefore variable and requires monitoring rather than assuming inevitable progression.
No, topical ropivacaine has not been shown to reduce overall post-tonsillectomy morbidity in pediatric patients.

A randomized controlled trial found no significant differences between topical ropivacaine and placebo in postoperative pain, analgesic requirements, nausea, vomiting, bleeding, or return to normal activity.
While some studies suggest modest early pain relief, the evidence does not support a broad reduction in morbidity.
No—c-kit (CD117) expression is not an established diagnostic marker for HBV-related chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma.
Some studies report increased c-kit immunostaining in cirrhosis and HCC compared with chronic hepatitis, but expression is variable and overlaps across these conditions.
It may have pathogenetic or prognostic interest, but it lacks the sensitivity and specificity needed for routine diagnosis.
Yes, the Supplemental Security Income program appears to reduce disability in the elderly.
Longitudinal studies such as the Health and Retirement Study have found that SSI receipt is associated with a significant reduction in disability among low-income elderly.
The likely mechanisms include poverty alleviation, improved access to health care, and better living conditions.
However, the evidence is not definitive and some confounding may remain.
The evidence is mixed.

In evolutionary and biomedical contexts, larger body size can offer advantages such as improved survival, competitive ability, and thermoregulation, but it also brings costs like higher metabolic demands, greater cancer risk (though Peto's paradox shows large species often evolve extra cancer defenses), and increased vulnerability to environmental change.

In humans, greater height is linked to some socioeconomic benefits but also to higher risks of certain cancers and possibly other diseases, with overall mortality effects being modest and context-dependent.
Thus, whether it is 'better' to be big depends on the species, environment, and which outcomes are measured.

Yes, laparoscopic (minimally invasive) foregut surgery is generally associated with a lower incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation than open foregut surgery in several observational studies and meta-analyses.
The reduction is thought to be due to less surgical trauma, pain, and systemic inflammation.
However, the evidence is not uniform across all foregut procedures, and some studies show no significant difference, so the effect is supportive rather than definitive.
No.
Wandering and physically nonaggressive agitation are overlapping but not equivalent constructs in dementia and geriatric psychiatry.

Physically nonaggressive agitation is a broader category that can include pacing, inappropriate dressing/undressing, repetitive handling of objects, and other motor behaviors, whereas wandering specifically refers to aimless or repetitive locomotion.
Wandering may occur without agitation and is often measured as a distinct behavioral symptom.
Yes.
Robotically assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy is less invasive than retropubic radical prostatectomy because it is performed through small abdominal ports rather than a large open incision.
It is generally associated with less blood loss, shorter hospital stay, and faster recovery, although cancer control and functional outcomes are broadly similar between the two approaches.
No.

Studies have not shown that confined placental mosaicism accounts for the adverse perinatal outcomes in IVF pregnancies; while it can occur more often in IVF/ICSI pregnancies and may cause placental dysfunction in some cases, it does not explain the overall increased risk, which is largely attributed to infertility, multiple gestation, and maternal factors.
Yes.
Kell alloimmunization in pregnancy is associated with fetal thrombocytopenia, in addition to causing severe fetal anemia.
This likely reflects suppression of erythroid and megakaryocytic progenitors.
The thrombocytopenia can increase bleeding risk and complicate intrauterine transfusion.
Yes—hormonal differences, particularly sex steroids, are largely responsible for the gender dimorphism after trauma-hemorrhage.

Studies show proestrus females with high estrogen have better immune, cardiovascular, and survival outcomes than males, while ovariectomy abolishes this advantage and testosterone is immunosuppressive.
Estrogen administration to males improves organ function and immune responses, supporting a causal hormonal mechanism rather than sex chromosome effects alone.
Evidence is mixed.

Specialty pharmaceuticals can deliver large clinical gains—such as cures for hepatitis C, disease-modifying therapies for rare disorders, and improved cancer outcomes—but their prices often exceed conventional cost-effectiveness thresholds.
Whether they are worth the price depends on the specific drug, indication, patient subgroup, and negotiated price; some are clearly cost-effective, while others are not.
Value-based pricing and outcomes-based contracts can help align price with benefit.
Yes.

Studies have found that medication history documentation in case notes varies significantly by admitting specialty, with general/internal medicine and geriatrics typically recording more complete histories than surgical or emergency specialties.
This variation likely reflects differences in training, workload, and perceived importance of medication review.
Nonetheless, recording is often incomplete across all specialties.
The evidence is mixed.

Some studies suggest that prolonging overall radiotherapy treatment time beyond about 8 weeks may reduce biochemical control, especially in high-risk prostate cancer, but many others show no significant effect, consistent with prostate cancer's low alpha/beta ratio and slow repopulation.
Therefore, while avoiding unnecessary treatment breaks is prudent, treatment duration is not a consistently established independent determinant of outcome.
Yes.
The ability to perform transurethral resection of the prostate is influenced by the surgeon's previous experience.
Less experienced surgeons generally have longer operative times, lower resection efficiency, and higher rates of complications such as bleeding, capsular perforation, and fluid absorption.
Outcomes tend to improve with increasing caseload, supervised training, and progression along the learning curve.
Yes, endothelin-1 likely contributes to hemodynamic changes during hemodialysis, mainly as a potent vasoconstrictor that counterregulates volume removal.
Plasma endothelin-1 often rises during dialysis due to shear stress, blood-membrane contact, and endothelial activation.
It has been linked particularly to intradialytic hypertension and vascular tone maintenance, while its role in intradialytic hypotension is less consistent.
Overall, the evidence supports a contributory but complex role rather than a sole cause.
The evidence is mixed.

Beta-adrenergic signaling is biologically important for clearing fetal lung fluid, and some small studies have suggested ADRB2 variants such as Gly16Arg and Gln27Glu may affect TTN risk, but other studies found no association with ADRB1/ADRB2 polymorphisms.
No ADRB genotype is established as a clinically useful risk factor for TTN.
No.
Severe macrosomia is not manifested at 11-14 weeks of gestation because macrosomia is defined by birth weight and becomes apparent later in pregnancy, typically in the second or third trimester.

First-trimester ultrasound at 11-14 weeks measures crown-rump length and nuchal translucency, and although early growth may correlate weakly with later overgrowth, it cannot diagnose or manifest severe macrosomia.
Therefore, severe macrosomia is not a feature of the 11-14 week scan.

Yes—a post hoc analysis of the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention (BIP) trial found that bezafibrate was associated with a significantly lower incidence of colon cancer in patients with coronary artery disease compared with placebo.
However, this was a secondary analysis with few events, so it does not definitively prove prevention and requires confirmation in dedicated trials.
Yes, there is evidence of an association, but it is mixed.
Many studies report higher serum homocysteine levels in people with vitiligo than in controls, sometimes linked to MTHFR polymorphisms or low folate/vitamin B12.
Other studies find no significant difference, so homocysteine may reflect oxidative stress or nutritional status rather than directly causing vitiligo.
Overall, the relationship is plausible but not definitively established.
Yes, the evidence suggests that risk factors for suicidal behavior differ somewhat by affective disorder polarity, though many are shared.

Bipolar disorder generally carries a higher suicide risk, with mixed states, earlier onset, rapid cycling, comorbid anxiety or substance use, and family history of suicide being particularly prominent.
In unipolar depression, prior suicide attempts, hopelessness, severe or recurrent episodes, comorbid anxiety or substance use, and psychosocial stressors are key risk factors.
Clinically, risk assessment should therefore consider polarity-specific factors while recognizing substantial overlap.
Yes, geriatric oncology consultation often modifies the cancer treatment plan for elderly patients.

Studies show that comprehensive geriatric assessment leads to changes in oncologic treatment decisions—such as reducing chemotherapy intensity, choosing surgery versus conservative management, or adding supportive care—in roughly 20–50% of cases.
These modifications are driven by factors like functional status, comorbidities, cognition, and patient preferences that are not captured by routine oncology evaluation.
Yes, but simply familiarizing surgeons with current evidence is often insufficient on its own.
It can lead to practice change when combined with active implementation strategies such as audit and feedback, reminders, local opinion leaders, or interactive educational sessions.
The magnitude of change varies by context, the strength of the evidence, and barriers to adoption.
Therefore, evidence familiarization is a useful but not guaranteed driver of practice change.
No.

While overweight children are more likely to become overweight adults, it is not inevitable; many normal-weight adults were overweight as children, and many overweight children do not remain overweight.
Risk depends on age, severity, duration of excess weight, family history, and lifestyle/environment.
So childhood overweight is a risk factor, not a guarantee.

No—vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VaIN) is biologically analogous to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) because both are HPV-driven squamous lesions, but their natural history and clinical evolution are not identical.

CIN, especially CIN 3, has a better-defined and generally higher risk of progression to invasive cancer, whereas VaIN is rarer, often multicentric or associated with prior CIN/hysterectomy, and has a less predictable course with lower but still real progression to vaginal cancer and frequent recurrence or persistence.
Thus VaIN is managed with similar principles but is not considered to have the same evolution as CIN.
Yes.

In the Dutch self-management intervention study, older patients who refused to participate were significantly older, more often female, had lower education, and reported worse self-rated health and more depressive symptoms than those who agreed to participate.
These differences suggest that trial participants were not fully representative of all eligible older patients.
Yes.
Cytokines such as interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α have been implicated in epilepsy and seizure generation.
They can promote neuroinflammation, increase neuronal excitability, and disrupt the blood-brain barrier.
Human and animal studies show cytokine changes in brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid after seizures, and anti-inflammatory approaches can reduce seizures in some models.
Yes.
